# Blog: Davy's — 155 years of sawdust and candles

Source: https://pintpoint.co.uk/blog/davys-wine-bars.html

Essay 3 August 2026 · London · Heritage

Davy's — 155 years of sawdust and candles

A family wine merchant that started off the Strand in 1870, opened the Boot & Flogger in a Southwark cellar in 1964 and helped define the modern London wine bar, and still lists fifteen London sites of its own — bars, cellars, wine-shop-tasting-rooms, a bar-and-grill and one specialist tobacconist, of which fourteen are actually trading — plus three El Vino sisters brought in in 2015. In 2007 the chain had 37 sites; more than half of the family-name ones have gone since.

In 2012, hanging under the BANGERS TOO pub sign at 1 St Mary at Hill, was a smaller sign in gold letters on black: Davys · Fine Wines and Eating. A year later the lease ran out, the pub closed, and 1 St Mary at Hill became a Bengali restaurant called Jamdani. The Davy's marque above the door came down with it.

That's the story of a lot of Davy's over the last fifteen years. The chain has been quietly editing itself down — closing sites, letting leases run out, folding branches into offices and restaurants. But it isn't gone. Fifteen sites are on Davy's own current listing (fourteen actually trading; the Crusting Pipe still on the page but closed since Christmas 2025), some of them in the same cellars they've been in for forty years, most of them still following the house formula: stone floors, candle stubs, port bottles racked to head height, and — if you know to ask — Old Wallop pulled through a hand pump. This is where that formula came from and what's left of it.

1870 — Rising Sun, off the Strand

Francis Edwin Davy opened The Rising Sun just off the Strand in 1870, calling it a "wine house." The site was chosen for its proximity to the new Charing Cross railway station and the trade the trains would bring — commuting City workers, day-trippers into town from Kent. In its first decades the business was more merchant than bar: FE Davy became a major shipper of Port, particularly for the London club trade, and in 1902 introduced the first of what the family still call their "own-label" wines. Those own labels remain, per the company's own account, "the cornerstone of our range" today.

Davy's is now on its fifth generation. The second (JHH Davy) took the business through the First World War and the General Strike of 1926. The third (SJE Davy) ran it through the Second — during which, per the company history, "customers had to bring their own glasses," and the original Barking cellars were lost in the Blitz. There is a photograph on the Davy's site of a lady scrubbing the front step of The Alfred's Head, 140 Newington Causeway, while men repair bomb damage behind her. The family kept trading.

1964 — the Boot & Flogger and the London wine-bar template

The fourth-generation head of the firm, John Davy, opened The Boot & Flogger on Redcross Way near London Bridge in 1964. Davy's own copy calls it "the birth of what would become the UK wine bar phenomenon," which oversells it — El Vino on Fleet Street had been going since 1879, the Ebury Wine Bar in Pimlico since 1959, and James Davy is honest about it in the Lander interview: this wasn't the founding of the movement so much as its most durable prototype. What Davy did was take a repeatable format — cellar, candles, port bottles racked to head height, house pours in pewter — and set it up as a proper chain. The Boot & Flogger was the seminal catalyst, not the origin.

Nor is the name a groan-worthy pub pun: a boot and a flogger are the two hand tools a Victorian merchant used to bottle wine by hand — the boot being the shoe that held the empty bottle upright, the flogger a mallet-like contraption that drove the cork home. Davy's runs on these small acts of vintners' literacy.

Getting the room open was the wrinkle. As John Davy put it — via James, in Lander's interview — "back then there were only three kinds of places to get a drink close to the City: the tea houses, pubs, which were strictly controlled by the brewers, and The Savoy. That was it." The brewery-influenced licensing magistrates weren't going to grant a wine bar; one reportedly told the family the room wasn't needed because "no wine bars existed at the time." Davy sidestepped the whole system by taking a free vintner's licence under his Vintners' Company membership — an ancient City freeman right that let him sell wine only, as a sole trader, within the City and along the historic port-route to the docks, without a magistrate's licence at all. The Boot & Flogger opened, poured, and the phrase "wine bar" entered the general London vocabulary in Davy's specific dialect. (The Redcross Way site is still there — technically owned personally by John Davy rather than the group.)

By the 1970s the wine-shop side of the business had been sold off to fund the bar rollout. The chain hit its stride in 1980, opening a site in newly-refurbished Covent Garden with, per the family history, "customers queued out of the door." Late-Thatcher London was a wine-bar city for about a decade — Davy's was the version of that scene that had actually been running the same room for a hundred years, not the version that had opened in a converted warehouse the year before. By 2007, when Nick Lander wrote up the chain for the FT (later republished on Jancis Robinson's site), the count was 37 wine bars and restaurants from Canary Wharf to White City — with the naming style at peak Davy's whimsy: Bung Hole Cellars, Skinkers, Tappit Hen, the Crusting Pipe. Which makes the 2025 loss of the Crusting Pipe land as something more than administrative attrition.

The Davy's formula

Every Davy's writes the same short list on the tin: stone-flagged floors, dark wood fittings, bottle racks and candlelight — that's the CAMRA description of Davy's at St James's, and it's transferable. Nick Lander, in that 2007 FT piece, called the interiors "the quintessential low-maintenance approach — spit and sawdust floors and empty bottles, of every possible size, on any available ledge and shelf." Sawdust used to be more literal than it is now; the phrase "sort of posh spit-and-sawdust," attributed to James Davy (fifth generation, currently at the helm) via Lander, does the job of two adjectives.

Their house ale is called Old Wallop. It used to be cask; since the pandemic it's mostly been on keg, though a Londonist visit to Truckles of Pied Bull Yard in 2009 caught the tail-end of the older regime — "imbibe Old Wallop from pewter tankards" — with Old Wallop still on the downstairs handpump before the pandemic-era keg shift. The pewter is real, not stagecraft; the pots are the tankards Davy's use, and the beer is cheaper by the four-pint jug than by the pint — a survival of vintners' economics from an era when the price of the vessel was part of the pour.

What was actually under the Old Wallop badge is one of those things that everyone-in-the-know knows and nobody-else-quite-does. The old City tankard pour was remembered by long-time regulars (and London CAMRA reporting of the era) as Courage Directors Bitter — 4.8% ABV, "Superior Ale" est. 1787 — but PINtPOINT's current profile for Davy's Old Wallop is lighter (4.2%, session-bitter rather than ESB), so today's beer may have drifted, been re-specified, or simply be recorded differently. Spitfire — Shepherd Neame, different brewery, different county — is a patron guess that turns up occasionally at the taps but isn't the answer for the classic City tankard pour.

The menu is very Davy's too, and famously has been forever. Four items — chicken liver pâté, a plate of Alderton ham from Suffolk with hot buttered potatoes, a plate of rare beef with the same, and treacle tart with clotted cream — have been on the card, Lander noted, "since the beginning." It's not gastropub cooking and it never has been; Lander's own verdict was that the wine, the pricing and the hospitality all outran the kitchen. The frame is wine-bar heritage, not culinary ambition, and that's the honest way to walk in.

The bar staff, at St James's and one or two of the others, still work in white shirts and ties. The room fills with what CAMRA politely calls a "largely besuited clientele." The visual signature — sawdust and candles, wood and bottle racks, port glasses on marble — has been so stable for so long that walking into one Davy's for the first time feels like walking back into a Davy's you've been to before, even if you haven't.

Bangers Too at 1 St Mary at Hill, EC3 — the last Christmas season before the lease ran out. Davy's ran the site for more than twenty years; by 2013 it was a Bengali restaurant. The hanging Davys · Fine Wines and Eating sign is visible under the pub sign. Photo: Ewan Munro, 2012 (used with permission).

The ghosts: Bangers, Boots and the slow thinning of Davy's

The Davy's brand ran two adjacent City sites for years, each named — with a house-style groan — "Bangers." Bangers Too at 1 St Mary at Hill was the Fenchurch Street one, running for the better part of two decades until its lease ran out in 2012; 1 St Mary at Hill became Jamdani the following year, and the shot above is from what was effectively the pub's farewell December. Bangers proper — Eldon House, 2–12 Wilson Street, EC2M — held on longer. It closed for the pandemic on 23 March 2020 and never reopened; the site was granted planning consent for office conversion and the pub was permanently closed in August 2021. A Tripadvisor review posted around then, mourning the closure, called it "one of the last 'real' Davys wine bars and restaurants in the City." That was the sound the brand made losing two of its bigger addresses in a decade.

The count now sits at fifteen Davy's-operated London sites on their own current tally (fourteen actually trading — the Crusting Pipe still on the page but closed since Christmas 2025), with three El Vino sisters alongside — and a ghost list that includes not just Bangers and the Crusting Pipe, but two different lives of the Tappit Hen name. Together they sketch the pattern of a shrinking chain — leases run out, sites redeveloped, revivals opened and let go, one entire Charing Cross classic reborn as a French bistro and then lost to lockdown.

The Crusting Pipe — lower ground floor of the Covent Garden market hall — closed on 21 December 2025, after 45 years. Opened 1980, it was one of the sites that rode the wine-bar boom in: a bright arched cellar under the piazza's pillars, house Port and a menu that leaned toward Iberian cured meats. Davy's cited "evolving trading environments and changing consumer habits", which is polite phrasing for a Covent Garden lease at Covent Garden money. The room is being taken by Mr Fogg's Tavern.

The City Boot ran for 41 years off the Barbican Highwalk at 7 Moorfields Highwalk EC2Y — a Davy's classic wedged into the elevated pedestrian network above London Wall — before the site was redeveloped in 2015. After a fifteen-month gap Davy's reopened it a short walk west, in a former El Vino bar at 3 Bastion Highwalk, 125 London Wall; the new City Boot opened in September 2016 and closed three years later, in September 2019. Two goes on the same stretch of Highwalk: the first ended by the developers, the second closed quietly, and CAMRA still lists the unit as "closed long-term, seeking new tenants".

City FOB , on Lower Thames Street EC3R under the Monument end of London Bridge, was the platonic 1980s City Davy's. The 1986 CAMRA guide caught it at full pomp: "exclusive rather pricey cellar bar, sawdust on the floor, wood seating, pints (no halves allowed) in pewter tankards. City dress only." It closed in 2010; the building still stands but the pub is gone.

Skinkers at 42 Tooley Street, just east of London Bridge, was another Lander-era City Davy's — one of the whimsy names on the 2007 list. Closed January 2013 to make way for the Network Rail redevelopment of London Bridge Station (the Shard-era rebuild swallowed a run of Tooley Street trade); CAMRA marked it permanently closed in March 2019, the site now restaurant use. The Ewan Munro Flickr shot of its hanging sign is the frontage image we have on file.

The Tappit Hen (Charing Cross) / Terroirs — 5 William IV Street WC2N — was the older and better-remembered of the two Tappit Hens Davy's have run. A deep-cellar Charing Cross classic; its vault level was specifically labelled "The Tappit Hen", after the old Scottish three-quart wine measurement. Davy's closed it as the Tappit Hen by mid-2007 (a Qype/Yelp review lamenting the loss still sits online, over eighteen years old). The site reopened in 2008 as Terroirs, a natural-wine French bistro that kept the atmospheric basement. Per CAMRA it closed 15 December 2020 in the second lockdown "future uncertain"; the permanent-closure notice landed June 2021.

The Tappit Hen (St Swithin's Lane) was the revival — Davy's took the name back in July 2019, opening a City version at 21–23 St Swithin's Lane just off the Bank end of Cannon Street (PA Life trade press covered the opening). It didn't last long: by the early 2020s the room had passed to Bar 1790, a Portuguese wine bar linked to the Sandeman house, which trades there now. For a strange couple of years, the revived Tappit Hen name at St Swithin's Lane overlapped with Terroirs still trading in the old Charing Cross Tappit Hen cellar — same lineage, two rooms, one recently reawakened name.

All nine are ghosts in PINtPOINT now, cross-linked back to their sites (and where relevant to their successor tenants — Mr Fogg's for the Crusting Pipe, Bar 1790 for the St Swithin's Tappit Hen) with archive photography where we have it and a "then / now" toggle so you can see them as they were and see what stands there today.

The fifteen Davy's still list

Davy's currently list fifteen non–El Vino London sites of their own — bars, cellars, wine-shop-tasting-rooms, a bar-and-grill and one specialist tobacconist — though that public list still includes the Crusting Pipe, which closed in December 2025. Not all fifteen fly the family name: the group runs bars under wine-cellar names (Grapeshots, Truckles, Boot & Flogger, Bunghole Cellars), a bar-and-grill (Factory House, in Leadenhall Market), retail shops with tasting bars (Davy's Wine Shop and Davy's Wine House, in Greenwich and Holborn) and even a specialist tobacconist (Segar & Snuff Parlour in Covent Garden). The full list, in the shape Davy's themselves publish:

- Davy's at St James's Crown Passage, SW1 · flagged floors, labyrinthine basement, formal dining above

- The Boot & Flogger Redcross Way, SE1 · the 1964 original, still trading

- Davy's Wine House + Bunghole Cellars 57 High Holborn, WC1V · the second-oldest Davy's site — ground-floor Wine House (wine shop + tasting bar), deep-basement Bunghole Cellars (wine bar & restaurant); both still branded distinctly on davy.co.uk today

- Truckles of Pied Bull Yard Bury Place, WC1 · one of central London's few beer gardens

- Champagne Charlies Villiers Street, WC2 · under the arches

- Mug House 1–3 Tooley Street, SE1 · near London Bridge

- Grapeshots Artillery Passage, E1 · off Bishopsgate

- Davy's Wine Vaults 161 Greenwich High Rd, SE10 · the Greenwich bar

- Davys Wine ShopGreenwich High Rd, SE10 8JA · the Greenwich retail shop, adjacent to the Wine Vaults

- Davy's at Plantation Place Fenchurch Street, EC3 · the eastern City survivor

- Factory House37 Leadenhall Place, EC3M · bar & grill in Leadenhall Market

- The Olde Wine Shades 6 Martin Lane, EC4R · Davy's-run wine house in a City lane

- Segar & Snuff Parlour27a The Market, WC2E 8RD · Covent Garden specialist tobacconist (the odd one on the list)

- Crusting Pipe (closed Dec 2025) Covent Garden · Davy's site still lists it as active; the room went to Mr Fogg's Market Tavern just before Christmas 2025 and stands under new tenancy now — the wine-bars page hasn't caught up

Fourteen of the fifteen appear to be actually trading; the fifteenth, the Crusting Pipe, remains on Davy's own site but has already passed into the ghost list above. One earlier version of this piece also cited Davy's Wine Bar at 201 Wood Lane W12 (Hammersmith) in the survivors list — that site is no longer on Davy's current wine-bars page. Investigation open on whether it closed, rebranded, or is no longer Davy's-operated; we'll ghost it once confirmed.

The El Vino sisters

Davy's acquired the El Vino group in 2015 — the Fleet Street institution and its sisters, run as sibling operations under the same ownership but with their own signage, menus and identity. Not pure-Davy's, but part of the same portfolio, and tagged chain:davys in PINtPOINT alongside the family-name sites so a chain filter surfaces both.

- El Vino Fleet Street 47 Fleet St, EC4A · the flagship since 1879, ex-Fleet-Street press canteen

- El Vino Blackfriars 30 New Bridge St, EC4V

- El Vino London Bridge 5a More Place, Tooley St, SE1 · More London side

All fifteen sites Davy's list (the fourteen currently trading, plus the Crusting Pipe which sits both on Davy's page and in the ghost list here), all three El Vinos and the historic Davy's ghosts carry a chain:davys tag in PINtPOINT; successor tenants such as Bar 1790 are linked through predecessor/successor relationships rather than treated as Davy's venues.

New · Curated Collection

Trace the survivors on the map

Every Davy's bar Davy's currently list, grouped by area — the City cluster, West End & Bloomsbury, South Bank, and Greenwich — now lives as Davy's Wine Bars, a Curated Collection in PINtPOINT. Not a crawl, not a route: a long-arc reference map to explore over weeks or months.

Open the collection →

Davy's vs Firkin — two ways to run a chain

The Davy's story sits alongside the Firkin one as two very different pillars of London chain drinking. Both used sawdust on the floor; they used it for opposite reasons.

Davy's (from 1870) is a traditional wine and ale house — candle-lit tables, private alcoves, house Port, Old Wallop in pewter tankards. Sophisticated, timeless, atmospheric. A family business that's still a family business.

Firkin (1979–2001) was the brewpub revolution — unpretentious, loud, boisterous neighbourhood locals; puns for names (Frog & Firkin, Pheasant & Firkin); Dogbolter brewed downstairs. David Bruce built it from one South London pub to 44 in fifteen years; the chain died when the brewing did.

Two iconic, contrasting pillars of London drinking culture — one still holding its rooms; the other now remembered as much for what it lost as for what it built.

Davy's has never been in a hurry, which is part of why it's still here. A chain that opens a handful of sites a decade and closes a handful more isn't chasing scale. It's tending a room that was old when the founder's grandson took it over, and passing it on. The stubs of candle in the wax rings on the shelf above the bar are the point, not the marketing. When a Davy's does close — as Skinkers did in 2013, Terroirs (the old Tappit Hen) in 2020, Bangers in 2021, the St Swithin's Tappit Hen revival not long after, and the Crusting Pipe just before Christmas 2025 — the room usually goes with it: the sawdust vacuumed up, the tankards packed off to the next site, the sign taken down. The 2012 shot at St Mary at Hill caught the sign coming down, though nobody knew it yet.

The fourteen still trading are, between them, most of the argument for why the chain outlasted the wine-bar boom. Not because they refused to change, but because the change was inside the room, not visible from the door.

# Blog: Ghosts of Baddow Brewery

Source: https://pintpoint.co.uk/blog/ghosts-of-baddow-brewery.html

Essay 30 August 2026 · Great Baddow · Essex pubs

Ghosts of Baddow Brewery

Baddow Brewery stopped brewing in 1927. Nearly a century later, 30 of the 61 pubs associated with it are still serving drinkers.

This is the sort of map PINtPOINT was made for: not just where to drink now, but where Essex used to drink.

There is a modern echo too. Chelmsford Brew Co now brews on Brewery Fields, a stone’s throw from the old brewing ground. The ghosts come first.

At 47 Church Street in Great Baddow stands The Old Brewery: the surviving shell of Baddow Brewery, a local brewing business whose story runs from the late eighteenth century through to the age of tied houses, consolidation and closure. The building is Grade II listed.

The headline history is simple enough. Baddow Brewery was founded in 1798 by a Mr Crabb. In 1866 Frederick and Arthur Veley came in as partners — later joined by Thomas Smee — and the firm ran as Crabb, Veley & Company until 1887. Two years after the Veleys arrived, in 1868, a new brewery was built to designs by George Scamell, a specialist brewery architect who had worked on Truman, Hanbury & Buxton's London plant earlier in the decade. From 1902 it was chaired by Reginald Watney, of the Watney brewing family, until his death in 1923. In 1927 it was acquired by Seabrook, and brewing at Great Baddow came to an end. Local oral history has fingered a specific culprit for the sale: the founder's three granddaughters, all staunch Temperance movement members.

But the more interesting story is not just the brewery building. It is the network.

The answer: 30 still appear to be trading

After working through the estate pub by pub, the current working count is:

30 Open*

14 Replaced

15 Closed

2 Unknown

That gives us a beautifully clean, slightly melancholy headline: of Baddow Brewery’s 61 listed pubs, 30 still appear to be trading. Not always under the same name. Not always with the same interior, ownership or beer. But still serving as pubs, bars, inns, hotels or pub-restaurants.

*Method note: “Open” includes renamed pubs, free houses, hotel bars and pub-restaurants such as Harvester — not only traditional wet-led locals.

Another 29 have ceased trading as pubs. Two remain unknown because the evidence is too thin to call honestly.

The survivors

The living half of the estate is the joy of the thing. But the names alone are not the story. The transformations are.

Four living transformations

- Coopers Arms → Hop Shop: a former tied house reborn as Chelmsford’s micropub culture.

- Crown, Hatfield Peverel → William B: old pub identity, new name, still serving.

- Nags Head, Moreton → Dog & Pickle: a renamed survivor with its own modern character.

- Five Bells, Vange → Harvester: not a traditional wet-led local, but still open, still licensed, still part of the living estate.

That is why the count matters. Baddow Brewery is dead as a brewery company, but its estate has not vanished. Half of it is still visible in the modern pub map; the other half survives as restaurants, shops, houses, names, rumours and awkward gaps in the record.

Curated Collection

Trace the survivors on the map

The thirty surviving pubs live on as Baddow Brewery Survivors — a Curated Collection in PINtPOINT. Not a crawl, not a route: a long-arc reference map, grouped by area, to explore over weeks or months. Two of the thirty (Bell Inn, Woodham Ferrers and Ship Hotel, Leigh-on-Sea) are trading but not yet on Untappd, marked as pending in the collection.

Open the collection →

The changed and the gone

Some former Baddow houses survive physically but no longer function as pubs. Some are restaurants, shops, homes, holiday lets or housing developments. Some appear to be simply closed. Some have left only a name in a directory and a stubborn gap on the map.

Sugar Hut deserves the spotlight here. The White Hart at Brentwood did not survive as a pub, but as Essex’s TOWIE nightclub it became something almost as map-defining: a former Baddow tied house reborn as reality-TV shorthand. The Bull at Pitsea gave its name to Bull Mews housing. That is what the gone half looks like too: not just disappearance, but mutation.

Replaced or converted

- Cross Keys, Moulsham Street — cinema, then retail

- Rose & Crown, Rainsford Road — housing

- Queens Head, Chelmsford High Street — retail

- Carpenters Arms, Great Baddow — Spice Lounge, formerly Yasmin

- Kings Head, Great Baddow — holiday let

- Cross Keys, Roxwell — Indian restaurant

- Admiral Rous, Galleywood — house

- Bell Inn, Little Waltham — house

- Black Lion, Althorne — house

- Cock Inn, Tillingham — house

- White Hart, Brentwood — Sugar Hut

- Old White Horse, Rayleigh — converted to Prezzo

- Bull Inn, Pitsea — Bull Mews housing

- Three Horseshoes, Billericay — retail

Closed or no longer trading

- White Horse, Townfield Street

- Anchor, Ingatestone

- New Ship Inn, Rochford

- Woolpack, Fryerning

- Harrows / Dick Turpin, A127

- Essex Arms, Chelmsford — not the Oddfellows Arms

- Bell Inn, Great Baddow

- New Found Out, Galleywood — building survives

- Carpenters Arms, East Hanningfield

- Wheatsheaf, West Hanningfield

- Plough, West Hanningfield

- Maltsters Arms, Willingale — building survives

- Butchers Arms, Woodham Ferrers

- Railway Hotel, Braintree

- Butchers Arms, Cold Norton — not The Norton

The two unknowns

The two awkward entries are Gardeners Arms, Kelvedon and New Inn, Pitsea.

Gardeners Arms is troublesome because ClosedPubs’ Kelvedon list and PubWiki both give fairly full Kelvedon lost-pub lists, and neither has a Gardeners Arms. Until a street, licensee or tithe entry turns up, it remains a name on a brewery list rather than a pinned house. New Inn, Pitsea is similarly polluted by other Essex New Inns, and the historic address is not yet nailed down tightly enough. So they stay unknown — not a failure of the map, but the map being honest.

Baddow brews again — but carefully

Chelmsford Brew Co now brews in Great Baddow. Their own account says the site had to be Brewery Fields, the landscape of the original Great Baddow brewery in the 1800s. CAMRA’s visit write-up placed them only a stone’s throw from the old Baddow Brewery, and the early BlueShack story has exactly the right local-brewery texture: family, garden-shed brewing, recipes getting out of hand.

Chelmsford’s current brewing scene is wider than one brewery — Radio City Beer Works and Brewhouse & Kitchen are part of it too — but the Great Baddow geography matters.

Not the same company. Not the old brewery building. But new beer on old brewing soil.

Research notes

- Brewery History Society Wiki: Baddow Brewery Co. Ltd

- Helen Gray, Goodness Grays: Baddow Brewery

- Chelmsford CAMRA: A Visit to Chelmsford Brew Company

- On the count: Brewery History records the 1927 Seabrook acquisition with 53 tied houses, while its pub list runs to 61 entries. This audit follows the full 61-name list and treats the 53 figure as the acquisition snapshot rather than the total research universe.

# Blog: Before Kick-Off: Why English Cask Has the Advantage

Source: https://pintpoint.co.uk/blog/before-the-final-cask.html

Essay 23 June 2026 · By Sophie Ro

Before Kick-Off: Why English Cask Has the Advantage

The football is heading to the business end. The Beer World Cup is heading the same way. And for the first time in a long time, English cask has a credible case to be the format that brings a trophy home — sixty years on from Wembley, with the Perfect Pint Promise barely a week old and the heritage cask category visibly back on the rise.

The argument works because it is not just a joke. Cask is the one beer format England can still claim without squinting: local, fragile, pub-dependent, and impossible to separate from the person keeping it properly in the cellar.

That is why the case for English cask at the Beer World Cup lands. Not because cask is cleaner, colder, stronger or more technically perfect than anything else. Because cask is the format that turns a pub into part of the beer.

So: who'd be in the line-up? An eleven-strong squad of properly kept cask beers. Why does that matter? Because warm, flat, hand-pulled bitter is the one beer category no other country dares compete in. Abroad it is a novelty. In Blighty it is a speciality.

Warm and flat, and neither

Cask is unfiltered, unpasteurised beer that finishes fermenting in the pub cellar, poured at cellar temperature with the carbonation that secondary fermentation gives it. Anywhere else those words are a fault report; here they are the format. The long version, with what the trade’s own numbers say about who is drinking it now, is in Cask Ale Week: the Format Nobody Else Can Pour.

Somebody checks the cellars

The Cask Marque Trust has been inspecting pub cellars for nearly thirty years, twice a year, by trained assessors — the plaque on the door, the sticker in the window, the listing in CaskFinder. Its beer-quality accreditation now trades under plainer language as the Perfect Pint Promise, and covers all draught rather than cask alone. What that promise is for is set out in Cask Ale Week: the Format Nobody Else Can Pour.

A category with a membership

Cask survived the 1970s because a consumer organisation argued for it: CAMRA, founded in 1971, and the Good Beer Guide, the festivals, the Pub of the Year network and fifty years of policy work that came with it. That membership is the moat, and no other beer category has one.

The Cask XI

So if England is going to make a serious case at a Beer World Cup, the team cannot be a squad of lager clones and international pale-ale lookalikes. Other countries do those brilliantly. Some do them better. England's strongest hand is older, stranger, softer and more pub-shaped: cask ale.

That is not just nostalgia. Cask carries English beer's heritage, history and stubborn local memory in a way no single modern style can. It depends on cellars, handpulls, throughput, publicans, regulars, regional breweries and the quiet skill of serving beer alive rather than merely cold. It is fragile, unfashionable in places, and easy to get wrong. But when it is right, it is the thing nobody else can quite copy.

That is why the England XI is all cask. Not because every English beer should be cask, and not because keg, lager or modern pale ale do not belong in English pubs. They do. But if the question is what England can send out against the world with the deepest roots and the clearest identity, the answer comes through a handpull.

So: who would we line up with? Eleven pints that, between them, cover the country properly. Not eleven shouts from the back. Eleven beers that any pub in any region would be lucky to have on. We have stayed away from the obvious pyramid of nostalgia — there are no team-sheet appearances for Greene King IPA or Cloudwater here — and stayed close to beers that still make sense on hand pump, in the kind of cellars Cask Marque exists to protect.

England · Starting XI

- Black Sheep Best Bitter — captain. Masham, and the other brewery in Theakston’s town, started by a Theakston who walked out of the family firm.

- Wadworth 6X — vice-captain. Devizes. Wiltshire’s everyday bitter, and the West Country’s default pint for a century.

- St Austell Tribute — Cornwall’s traveller: the pale that made it out of the county and onto bars everywhere east of it.

- Sharp's Doom Bar — Rock, Cornwall. The one Landlord has only just overtaken, and still on more bars than almost anything.

- Boddingtons (cask) — Manchester, via J.W. Lees, and back on hand pump since 2025. The keg widget version isn't this beer.

- Adnams Ghost Ship — Southwold. Suffolk's quiet diplomat, and the one that wins the under-thirties.

- Theakston Old Peculier — Masham. Fifth-generation family brewing, and the one for a winter goal.

- Hook Norton Hooky Bitter — Oxfordshire, from a tower brewery that still runs on steam. Perennial Cask Marque favourite.

- Brakspear Bitter — Henley by birth, Witney by address. Bone-dry, double-dropped, faintly orange-peel.

- Marston's Pedigree — Burton. The Unions are gone; the beer endures. Pedigree by name and nature.

- Adnams Broadside — Southwold's other one. Strong, malty, Trafalgar-named, and there to anchor a back four.

Bench: Fuller’s London Pride, Timothy Taylor’s Landlord, Draught Bass, Harvey’s Sussex Best. The famous four, held back because everyone already knows what they can do. Caledonian Deuchars IPA would have started, but plays for Scotland.

What this team has that others don’t

Look down the eleven. Every one is from a region, a brewery town, a pub network, or a drinker memory that still means something. Several are still family-owned; the rest sit inside larger portfolios where the commercial logic is now plain: do not mess with the thing drinkers came back for.

That is the moat, and it is a matter of format rather than age: Belgium has older brewers and Germany older breweries, but only cask has to be finished in the cellar of the pub that serves it. The full version of that argument, and what it means for who is drinking cask now, is in Cask Ale Week: the Format Nobody Else Can Pour.

And now the big brewers want the old names

Heritage cask has become heritage IP: Damm has bought the Old Speckled Hen family from Greene King, J.W. Lees has Boddingtons back on cask, Allsopp’s and Double Diamond are being revived, and Draught Bass is on more than a thousand hand pumps again. Flattering, and slightly dangerous — the handpull is fashionable again, and the awkward bit is who owns the badge above it.

Where to drink the Cask XI

Most of the eleven travel into London freehouses; the rest are easy to find in their home regions. PINtPOINT lists pubs serving each one by venue — the simplest way to organise an evening is to pick a player and let the venue list do the rest. The harder pints are honest about themselves: Boddingtons in genuine cask is rare, and the Whippet's J.W. Lees-brewed hand pull is one of the few places in London you will get it.

If you want to do it properly, look for the plaque on the way in. With the Beer World Cup conversation already loud, that promise feels overdue.

Find pubs near you on PINtPOINT

Sixty years on

Football has not been kind to England for a long time. The Beer World Cup might be kinder, if we write the rules right and play the format we have. Sixty years since 1966 sounds like a long time. It is. It is also the same span of time over which British cask went from a near-extinct format to a community-owned category, defended by a membership organisation, audited by an independent standard, and now relaunched as a consumer promise the rest of the world cannot copy.

That is something to argue for. Loudly. The final whistle is still to come.

Cask Ale Week runs 17–27 September. The cellars are getting ready.

P.S. — a clutch of British brewers have brewed tournament-specific specials for this exact moment. None qualify for the heritage Cask XI (they are days old, not decades) but all worth a flag if you spot one on a hand pump in the next few weeks: Greene King's 60 Years of Hurst (4% golden pale, made with Sir Geoff Hurst MBE, 5p from every pint to Diverse Abilities); Iron Pier's 1966 (4.7% Manchester Bitter, historic recipe from England's victorious World Cup year, spotted on hand-pull this week at the Hopper's Hut in Kent); Bradfield's Farmers World Cup Ale (4.2% pale hoppy, sold in 9-gallon casks); Norfolk Brewhouse's Skipper World Cup Special (4.2% best bitter, transatlantic hop blend); Woodforde's Route to 1966 (3.4% session pale, grapefruit and lemon); Saltaire's Golden Boot (4.8% English pale ale, citrus and orange peel, limited edition); and Milestone's World Cup Gold (4.5% golden ale, orange and tangerine notes). The names alone tell you what every British brewer is reaching for: the 1966 anniversary.

FAQ

Why does CAMRA still matter?
CAMRA — the Campaign for Real Ale — has been the consumer organisation that argues for properly kept living beer since 1971. Without it, much of what survives as British cask might not. The Good Beer Guide, local festivals, the Pub of the Year network and decades of policy work on pub protections are CAMRA's work. The community is the reason cask still exists at the scale it does.

Where can I find the Cask XI?
Most of the eleven are well-distributed in their home regions and travel into London freehouses. PINtPOINT lists pubs serving each by venue. Boddingtons in cask is rarer — the Whippet in EC2 keeps a hand-pulled version contract-brewed by J.W. Lees in Manchester.

Companion essays: Beer World Cup XI — the manifesto · All 48 squads · Wall chart — Fixtures & results

- Cask Marque Trust — cask-marque.co.uk

- Campaign for Real Ale — camra.org.uk, the Good Beer Guide, the Champion Beer of Britain register

- Des de Moor, Cask: The Real Story of Britain's Unique Beer (CAMRA Books, 2023)

- Phil Mellows, Morning Advertiser — "The classic heritage brands making a comeback", 16 June 2026

# Blog: Cask Ale Week: the Format Nobody Else Can Pour

Source: https://pintpoint.co.uk/blog/cask-ale-week-2026.html

Essay 17 September 2026

Cask Ale Week: the Format Nobody Else Can Pour

Cask Ale Week runs from 17 to 27 September, and it celebrates the one thing British beer cannot ship abroad: unfiltered, unpasteurised beer that finishes fermenting in the cellar of the pub you drink it in. The publican is part of the recipe, which is why nobody else has copied it, and why a bad one tastes like an apology.

Thirteen pints worth chasing this week, what the plaque on the door actually promises, and the numbers behind a revival that is being led, of all people, by drinkers in their twenties.

The misconception we keep apologising for

Anywhere else in the world, you would read warm and flat on a back-of-bottle review and put the glass down. In Britain, that combination — given a working cellar and a publican who knows what they are doing — is the format. Cask ale is not a fault. It is unfiltered, unpasteurised beer that finishes its fermentation inside the cask, in the pub cellar, under the publican's care. It is poured at cellar temperature, around 11 to 13 degrees, which is cool to the touch but not cold to the tongue. Its carbonation comes from secondary fermentation and a soft natural release, not a CO2 cylinder.

This is what makes cask hard to copy. A keg lager travels. A bottle of Bordeaux travels. A cask of bitter, properly kept, is a living thing that exists for a few days in one specific cellar, on one specific bar, in one specific pub. It cannot be exported as a product. It can only be drunk in place. The technical window is small — Des de Moor's recent book on cask puts the ideal serving window at three days once broached, four with very careful cellar work — but the cultural consequence is huge. That makes it the most local format the global drinks industry has, and the easiest to lose, which is why the people who care about it care so loudly.

Who is actually drinking it

This is the biggest one yet: more than 10,000 pubs have signed up, with hundreds of breweries, a million free tasters between them, and an app trail that pays out in a T-shirt after twelve pints. The organisers are making a point with the number, because the trade needs the encouragement.

The audience is changing underneath it. CGA’s June figures put 16% of cask drinkers between 18 and 34, and the Society of Independent Brewers reports a quarter of 18 to 24-year-olds have now tried cask, up ten per cent on the year, with some independents seeing cask growth in double digits.

Firebrand Brewing in Cornwall is one of them, at 18% up on the year. Its founder Joe Thomson told The Drinks Business that drinkers "seem to be embracing cask in a way we've not seen for years", and marked the week by brewing a 4.8% pale ale from an 1864 recipe: pale malt, Goldings, nothing else. The reasons younger drinkers give are not the ones the trade expected either. Most cask is under 4.5%, it cannot be delivered to your door, and it is the cheapest proper pint on the bar: £4.54 against £4.97 for the average pint.

None of which means the category is fixed. Cask still sells 8.1% of draught beer by volume and only 7.4% by value, volumes are falling where distribution has been cut, and a week of celebration does not reverse a decade. The cheapness is the sore point in the trade. St Austell's chief operating officer Andrew Turner put it plainly to the Morning Advertiser in July: cask is "the most difficult beer to look after, requires the most energy, the most effort, but yet it appears to be the cheapest pint on the bar — and the two just don't go hand in hand." He expects it to be the trendiest drink on the bar again; he would rather it arrived with a price that paid for the cellar work.

What the plaque on the door promises

Cask Ale Week was started in the early 2000s by the Cask Marque Trust, the body behind the plaques and window stickers you have been walking past for years, and it runs with CAMRA and most of the trade behind it. Any pub can take part, Cask Marque member or not; the campaign names a Beer of the Day and a Brewery of the Day, and lists what is on near you.

For nearly thirty years, the Cask Marque Trust has been doing the quiet work of independently assessing British pub cellars: twice-yearly, by trained beer professionals, with a star rating that publicans actually compete on. The plaque on the door, the sticker in the window, the listing in the CaskFinder app — all from the same accreditation pipeline.

The trust's beer-quality accreditation — what used to be Beer Marque — has had its consumer-facing rebrand. It is now the Perfect Pint Promise , with a single line at the top of the page that should have been there years ago: your guarantee of a quality pint every time. Not a brewery marketing badge. Not a sponsorship deal. An independent standard you can trust. And it isn't a cask-only badge — PPP tests all draught: cask, keg, lager, stout, cider, no/low.

The point of the rebrand is what it says out loud. Beer Marque told you a pub had passed an inspection. Perfect Pint Promise tells you what the inspection is for: that the next pint you pull out a chair for is going to be in good nick. That is a much easier sentence to hear in a busy bar.

The infrastructure scales with the ambition. The Cask Marque Trust audits 7,000 5-star cellars right now; the Perfect Pint Promise aims for 3,000 fully accredited venues inside twelve months. The standard hardens at the same time — Beer Pro e-learning for bar staff, proper pour, correct glassware. The point isn't just the cellar any more. It is the whole pub.

The plaque is the same. The CaskFinder app is the same. The decades of cellar audits behind it are the same. What changed is the language at the front of the bar, and it is sharper.

CAMRA, real ale, and a community that did the work

None of this would still exist without CAMRA. The Campaign for Real Ale was founded in 1971 by four men in a Kerry pub who thought British brewing was being homogenised into oblivion. They were right. Most of British brewing in the 1970s was being homogenised into oblivion. Cask survived because a consumer organisation argued for it, year after year, in front of policy makers, brewers, MPs and drinkers who had been told their preferred format was over.

The Good Beer Guide is CAMRA's. Local beer festivals are CAMRA's. The annual Pub of the Year network is CAMRA's. Decades of work on pub protections — on planning consent, on the tied-pub Statutory Code, on the small brewers' duty relief, on stopping the conversion of pubs into supermarkets — is CAMRA's. So is the community that turns up to drink the beer.

That community is the actual moat. Cask ale is the most consumer-defended product in British drink. Other categories have lobby groups; cask has a membership. 150,000 paid-up members carrying around a guidebook and an opinion is a different kind of asset to a marketing budget.

Thirteen pints for the week

Not the thirteen best cask ales in Britain. Nobody could agree that list, and half of it would be a beer brewed eight miles from your house in numbers too small to find. These are the ones you can actually walk in and order: widely distributed, kept by pubs that know them, and between them covering most of the country. A pub with any of these on the bar is a pub that has bothered.

The better pint this week is probably the local you have never heard of, poured by someone who cares. Ask what is going well. These thirteen are what to do when nobody offers.

Thirteen to look for

- Fuller's London Pride — now under Asahi, but still carrying one of English cask's most recognisable badges. The London bitter against which all other London bitters are measured. Bready, biscuity, brilliantly drinkable. Hammersmith via every freehouse south of the Thames.

- Timothy Taylor's Landlord — Keighley. The pint that converts lager drinkers back. Four times Champion Beer of Britain, and now the biggest seller in cask.

- Greene King Abbot Ale — Bury St Edmunds. At 5% the strong end of a session, and one of the most widely poured cask ales in the country, which is its own kind of achievement. Fruitcake and bitterness, everywhere from village locals to city chains.

- Draught Bass — the Burton one. Now contract-brewed for AB InBev's Budweiser UK at Carlsberg's Marston's site in Burton, but kept alive by a drinker network that maps every pump in the country. The pump count tripled this year, from 350 outlets to over a thousand. Cask Drinker Network. National Bass Day. The hand-pulls are coming back.

- Harvey's Sussex Best — Lewes. The proof that a small regional brewer with a single town's worth of conviction can produce one of the great session pints. Bitter that tastes like the South Downs.

- Boddingtons (cask) — Manchester, via J.W. Lees. Relaunched as cask in 2025 — 150 Greater Manchester outlets first, 400 nationally by January 2026, now 15% of Lees's total production. The Whippet in EC2 is one of London's. Cask only. The keg widget version isn't this beer.

- Adnams Ghost Ship — Southwold. Pale, citrus-hopped, modern enough to win the under-thirties without losing the cask faithful. Suffolk's quiet diplomat.

- Thornbridge Jaipur — Bakewell. Often called Britain’s first craft IPA, and 5.9% of proof that the argument between cask and craft was always a false one: it is at its best pulled through a handpump. Twenty-one years old this year, and still the one people remember.

- Theakston Old Peculier — Masham. North Yorkshire's strong dark ale, fifth-generation family-brewed, never not on form. The one for a cold night. If the pub has XB as well — 4.5%, ruby, first brewed in 1982 and named after the letters chalked on the cask — order that instead.

- Hook Norton Hooky Bitter — Oxfordshire. Brewed in a Victorian tower brewery that still uses steam. Perennial Cask Marque favourite. The pint you forget about until it is in front of you.

- Brakspear Bitter — Henley-on-Thames originally, now brewed at Wychwood in Witney. Bone-dry, double-drop fermented, faintly orange-peel. One of the oldest classic English bitter recipes still on a working hand pump. Dry enough to keep you on it all evening.

- Marston's Pedigree — Burton. The Burton Union system kept it alive for decades; the system is gone now but the beer endures. Pedigree by name and nature.

- Adnams Broadside — Southwold's other one. Strong, malty and Trafalgar-named: Ghost Ship's older brother.

Thirteen is an arbitrary number. Four more that would have done the same job: Butcombe Original , Oakham Citra , Titanic Plum Porter , Caledonian Deuchars IPA — the last of which is Edinburgh’s, and a reminder that cask did not stop at the border.

Why nobody else has this

Look down the list. Every one of them is from a region. None began life as a multinational product-board exercise. Every one is rooted in a region, a brewery town, a pub network, or a drinker memory that still means something. Several are still owned by the families or regional breweries that made them; others now sit inside larger corporate portfolios, where the commercial logic is increasingly clear: do not mess with the thing drinkers came back for.

That is the moat. No other country has a network of this size. Ireland keeps cask alive too, and Northern Ireland is on the Cask Ale Week map; nowhere else has thousands of pubs running it as the house format. The closest analogues — Belgian Trappist abbey ales, German Rauchbier in Bamberg, Czech tank lager in Prague — are formats that travel through bottles or kegs. Cask travels only into the cellar of the pub down the road. It is a deeply, irreducibly local thing, and Britain is the country that built a national network of pubs willing to run it.

Three ways to be old, three ways to claim heritage. Belgium have the oldest brewers — Rochefort has been brewing continuously since 1595, with abbey lineage back to 1230. Germany has the oldest breweries — Weihenstephan dates itself to 1040, and Munich’s oldest, Augustiner, to 1328. England have the oldest format. Only one of those three definitions of old can be poured, kept and drunk locally without first being shipped, filtered or pasteurised.

The big brewers have noticed

There is another reason this suddenly feels current. Heritage cask is no longer just something CAMRA members defend and regional brewers quietly keep alive. The big brewers have noticed the ghosts on the pub wall are worth money. It has the faintly familiar feel of craft beer a decade ago: once the independents proved the appetite was real, the larger players moved in for the brands, the credibility and the route to market.

Damm, best known in Britain for Estrella, has bought the Old Speckled Hen family from Greene King. JW Lees has brought Boddingtons back on cask. Allsopp's and Double Diamond are being revived. Draught Bass is on more than a thousand hand pumps again. Timothy Taylor's Landlord has overtaken Doom Bar at the top of the cask pile — Morning Advertiser's 2026 Drinks List puts Landlord ahead on both volume and value.

That is flattering, and slightly dangerous. It proves the category has cultural pull again. It also means cask is being rediscovered not only as beer, but as heritage IP: names, mirrors, pump clips, memories, and pub-wall ghosts that can be reactivated once the market is ready.

The handpull is fashionable again. The awkward bit is who owns the badge above it.

Where to drink it this week

Most of the thirteen travel into London freehouses; the rest are easy to find in their home regions. PINtPOINT lists the pubs serving each one, so the simplest way to organise an evening is to pick a beer and let the venue list do the rest. The harder pints are honest about themselves: Boddingtons in genuine cask is rare, and the Whippet in EC2 is one of the few places in London that has it.

If you want to do it properly, pick a Perfect Pint Promise pub — same Cask Marque Trust accreditation, plainer language on the door: that the pint you order will be in good nick.

Find pubs near you on PINtPOINT

Eleven days

None of this makes a badly kept pint taste better. It does mean that when you find a good one this week, someone in a cellar earned it.

Cask Ale Week runs to 27 September. The cellars are ready.

FAQ

What is cask ale?
Cask ale — also called real ale — is unfiltered, unpasteurised beer served from a hand pump or by gravity. Conditioning finishes inside the cask in the pub cellar, which makes the publican as important as the brewer. It is poured cool rather than cold and carries softer, natural carbonation. There is nothing wrong with the beer; it is meant to be like that.

Is Cask Marque the same as the Perfect Pint Promise?
The Cask Marque Trust runs the Perfect Pint Promise. It is the trust's beer-quality accreditation, formerly called Beer Marque, renamed to make the consumer guarantee clearer. The trust has been assessing pub draught quality for almost thirty years; the plaque, the CaskFinder app and the audits are the same lineage. The Perfect Pint Promise covers all draught — cask, keg, lager, stout, cider, no/low — not cask alone.

Is cask ale really warm and flat?
Cellar temperature, not warm. Lightly carbonated by secondary fermentation, not flat. Served as the brewer intended. The descriptors are anywhere-else fault sheets; in Britain they are a category.

Sources

- Cask Marque Trust — cask-marque.co.uk

- Des de Moor, Cask: The Real Story of Britain’s Unique Beer (CAMRA Books, 2023)

- Morning Advertiser — Andrew Turner of St Austell on cask’s price, 2 July 2026, and Landlord’s cask lead, 19 June 2026; Phil Mellows on the heritage brands, 16 June 2026

- The Drinks Business, 14 September 2026 — Firebrand’s 18% uplift, and SIBA’s Independent Beer Report behind the 18-24 figures

# Blog: September is Oktoberfest

Source: https://pintpoint.co.uk/blog/september-is-oktoberfest.html

Essay 18 September 2026 · Beer history · Festivals

September is Oktoberfest

The Wiesn opens tomorrow at noon and runs until 4 October. It began 216 years ago, in 1810, but this is only its 191st edition: Oktoberfest has been officially cancelled 26 times. At midday the Lord Mayor of Munich taps the first keg in the Schottenhamel tent and shouts “O’zapft is!” — a ritual the festival has kept since 1950 — and only then does the beer start flowing.

When most people picture Oktoberfest they think of lederhosen and dirndls, oompah bands, litre steins, bratwurst, schnitzel and sauerkraut. They also assume it happens in October and that the beer is M&auml;rzen. The reality is a little different.

The name has travelled further than almost any other in beer — to Brazil, to Ontario, to Ohio, to a Methodist mission hall on Peter Street in Manchester. Say “Oktoberfest” in four countries and you will not be handed the same drink twice — and the oldest of them is not the one in Munich. Munich quietly changed it decades ago, from the amber M&auml;rzen to the pale, dry Festbier now poured in the tents.

Munich changed the beer, and kept the name

The festival beer used to be dark — closer to a Munich dunkel than to anything poured in the tents now. The turn came in 1872. A hot summer had run the festival’s cellar dry, and Michael Schottenhamel put on a Vienna-style beer instead — brewed by the Franziskaner-Leist brewery, where Josef Sedlmayr had spent a year working the style up, and sold as Ur-Märzen. Märzen for the month it was made in: brewed in March, before summer brewing stopped, and lagered through the warm months to be drunk in autumn. It was stronger and dearer than the beer it replaced, and it sold out. Bock-strength festival lagers held on until the First World War, and between the wars the beer wandered anywhere from 4% to 9%, settling into the reddish-brown colour the world now calls Märzen.

Then Munich moved again. Over the second half of the twentieth century its brewers lightened the festival beer into the pale, dry Festbier the tents pour today — a beer engineered to be drunk by the litre for sixteen days. It is an excellent beer and a genuine piece of engineering. It is also not what was in the Schottenhamel tent in 1890.

So the most traditional festival in beer is pouring its newest recipe, and has been for fifty-odd years.

For the geeks: Märzen v Festbier

Both are lagers made with German hops. The difference is the malt.

Märzen

Festbier

Colour

Amber to copper

Deep yellow to gold

Base malt

Munich and Vienna

Pilsner, with a little Vienna or Munich

Taste

Toasted bread crust, malt-sweet, clean finish

Lighter and drier; the hops show a little more

Body

Medium to full, but not heavy

Medium, and very easy to drink

The pale one is not the weaker one. Festbier runs to about 6%, the same as a Märzen, but without the Munich malt’s weight and sweetness it drinks like an ordinary Helles of around 5% — which is how a litre of it catches people out.

American “Oktoberfest” beers keep the amber one, often with caramel malts Munich never used. In Munich only six breweries may pour at the Wiesn, and what they pour in the big tents is Festbier, not Märzen.

The six

Wiesn beer

Worth knowing

Augustiner

6.3%

Munich’s oldest brewery, founded 1328, and the only one still pouring from 200-litre wooden barrels

Hofbräu

6.3%

The Staatliches Hofbräuhaus: owned by the Bavarian state, as the name says

Löwenbräu

6.1%

The one with the roaring lion outside its tent

Paulaner

6.0%

The youngest of the six; its monks served their first beer in 1634

Hacker-Pschorr

6.0%

Still pours an amber Märzen from the wood in Poschner’s, a small tent

Spaten

5.9%

Poured in the Schottenhamel tent, so it fills the first stein; the first brewery to sell a Munich Helles, in 1894

America kept the beer Munich abandoned

The country with no historical claim on the festival at all is the one that preserved its beer. The American Oktoberfest is a Märzen: amber to deep copper, malt-forward, bread crust and caramel and toffee, typically 5–6% — a shade stronger, sweeter and more caramelised than the German article, and often carrying more hop bitterness than German brewers would bother with.

The keepers of the flame are doing it properly. Jack's Abby's Copper Legend is built on imported Pilsner, Vienna and Munich malts and decoction-mashed, which is a laborious old-world technique nobody adopts by accident. Shiner's Oktoberfest runs Munich and caramel malts against Hallertau Tradition and Hersbrucker hops. Neither is chasing what Munich is pouring. Both are brewing what Munich used to pour, thousands of miles from the field where Munich stopped pouring it.

And now one of them has crossed over

Here is the part that makes 2026 worth writing down. Firestone Walker’s Oaktoberfest was a Märzen-style lager of Vienna and Munich malts, part-fermented in oak barrels — a thoroughly Californian way to treat a Bavarian style, and a beer they built a season around. This year they have switched to a 6% golden Festbier brewed with Mahrs Bräu of Bamberg, on Bamberger Pilsen malt, and in their own words inspired by the modern Festbiers poured in the tents of Munich. An American brewery that built a season on the old beer has just gone to Bavaria for the new one.

Sierra Nevada’s is not the same thing, whatever the timing suggests. Theirs is golden and 6% this year, brewed with Hoppebräu of Waakirchen, but they have been making a German-collaboration Festbier for years and rotating the partner each time. That is a passport stamp, not a conversion. Jack’s Abby and Shiner, meanwhile, have not moved an inch.

So the flip is real and it is narrow. Munich pours the new beer. America kept the old one — and the brewery that built a season on it has just brewed the other.

Britain chose both

You would expect the exports to be the nostalgic ones. For half of Britain it is the other way round: the importers are the most Munich-faithful room of the lot.

Albert’s Schloss opens its Oktoberfest tomorrow — the same morning as the Wiesn — and runs to 25 October across Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham and Soho, pouring all six Munich Oktoberfest breweries across tap and tank. Not beers in the style of the Wiesn. The actual Wiesn beers, which means the pale modern Festbier, which means Manchester is drinking exactly what Munich is drinking.

Head of Steam are running theirs for exactly the Wiesn’s sixteen days, 19 September to 4 October: German beer, two-pint steins, pretzels and live music. Both chains open on the same Saturday as Munich; only one of them stops when Munich does.

Then there is the other half, brewing its own — and this is where the vocabulary stops meaning anything and starts being fun. Polly’s in north Wales went out last autumn at 5.7% with a can called Festbier – Märzen: both answers at once, the two beers this whole piece is about printed on one can. This year’s is announced and not yet poured. Verdant, in Cornwall, have brewed all three — a Dunkel, a smoked Märzen and a Festbier — and are throwing their own Oktoberfest on Saturday: the festival’s whole history in three cans. Indie Rabble, in Windsor, open on the same Saturday as Munich with Löwenbräu’s and Hacker-Pschorr’s Oktoberfestbiers on tap and the first pour of their own 5.2% Märzen beside them: the modern answer and the old one, a few feet apart.

The events go the same way. RedWillow’s Lager & Sausage festival opens on Park Green in Macclesfield on Saturday at noon — the same hour as the Wiesn — with a ceremonial cask tapping and an oompah band: Munich’s opening ritual, transplanted into a vessel Munich would not recognise.

Which is the clue to what Britain is actually doing. Fyne Ales, at Cairndow in Argyll, call theirs a Bavarian Fest Bier: 5.5%, amber to chestnut, with a little cherrywood-smoked malt in it, unfiltered and naturally settled — and they rack it into cask. It is brewed by Yvonne Wernlein, a third-generation German brewer, as a tribute to the cask beers of Franconia. A German, in Scotland, sending a festival lager out through a handpump.

Put like that, the cask is the whole British argument in one vessel. Munich’s Festbier is built to be cold, bright and briskly carbonated, drunk fast by the litre. Pull a festival lager soft and settled at cellar temperature and you have changed the beer before anyone has argued about the recipe — which, given that two centuries of Oktoberfest consist of exactly that manoeuvre, is less a liberty than an inheritance. Yesterday, during Cask Ale Week, we made the case for the handpump as the thing Britain kept. This is the same argument from the other end: the most traditional festival in beer quietly stopped keeping its own.

None of it is preservation and none of it is replication. America kept a style; Munich engineered one; Britain treats the whole German festival vocabulary as a licence — borrow the words, brew what you fancy, tap a cask, book the oompah band. Given that the festival’s own history is a story of quietly changing the recipe and keeping the name, that may be the most Bavarian behaviour on offer.

The festival travelled further than the beer

The name has outgrown the beer entirely in places. Blumenau in Santa Catarina has run one since 1984; Kitchener–Waterloo in Ontario bills itself as Canada’s Greatest Bavarian Festival; Oktoberfest Zinzinnati in Cincinnati, first held in 1976, is holding its fiftieth this very weekend. All three draw crowds in the high hundreds of thousands.

All three are billed as the biggest Oktoberfest outside Germany. They count differently enough that the contest cannot be settled, and the winner was never the interesting part. Three separate countries, each certain it is holding the real thing, in a festival whose home city quietly changed the recipe.

Oktoberfest isn’t really in October

It was not a harvest festival. It was a wedding. On 12 October 1810, Crown Prince Ludwig married Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen and Munich was invited to the party on the fields outside the city gates — fields still named the Theresienwiese after the bride, which is why Germans call the whole thing the Wiesn. The only event was a horse race. The agricultural show, the part that makes it look like a harvest festival, was bolted on the following year.

It is not really in October either. Drinkers had been complaining about the Bavarian cold since the 1820s, so the festival was walked steadily forward into the milder end of September, and by around 1905 it had settled there for good. It keeps the name by finishing on the first Sunday in October — the 4th, this year — which means that of the sixteen days of the 191st Oktoberfest, twelve of them fall in September. The one thing everybody thinks they know about the festival, that it is the October one, has been wrong for over a century.

Nor was the beer ever fresh. A Märzen is, by definition, the oldest beer in the cellar rather than the newest — brewed in March, drunk in October. A festival celebrating the harvest by serving the previous spring's beer is not a harvest festival, it is a clearing-out. The genuinely harvest-fresh beer in this story is green hop — hops in the copper within twelve hours of being picked — and nobody has built a sixteen-day festival on it, because you cannot: it is gone in a fortnight.

So the month is wrong, the harvest was never there, and the beer was chosen for having sat still the longest. Almost nothing about Oktoberfest is what most people think it is.

The one thing that travelled intact

For all that, there is one part of Oktoberfest that travelled, and it is not in the glass. In the Munich tents, two or three times an hour, the band stops whatever it is playing and starts Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit. A few thousand people put down their conversations, pick up a litre of beer and sing a toast to Gemütlichkeit, a word English has never managed to import: warmth, ease, the specific contentment of being among people with no particular need to be anywhere else. Then comes the count — Oans, zwoa, drei, g'suffa! One, two, three, drink — and the room drinks together.

That is Munich’s clock, and the clock did not travel. The song did. They sing Ein Prosit in Blumenau, in Kitchener, in Cincinnati, and in that Manchester mission hall at teatime — some rooms often, some when the mood takes them, none of them translating it. Every country in this piece changed the beer. Not one of them changed the words. The festival was never really about a recipe. It was about the interval at which strangers agree to become a crowd, and that exports beautifully, in any colour of lager you like.

There isn’t one Oktoberfest any more.

Source material

- oktoberfest.de — the 191st Oktoberfest, 19 September to 4 October 2026, the six breweries and their Wiesn beers, and the Wiesn barometer if you would rather not queue

- American Homebrewers Association: the history of beer at Oktoberfest — the 1872 hot summer and the drift from dark lager to Märzen

- HISTORY: the origins of Oktoberfest — the 1810 wedding, the horse race, and the agricultural show added the following year

PINtPOINT currently lists over 350 beers tagged as Festbier, Märzen or Oktoberfest. Found one we’re missing? Paste the Untappd link into PINtPOINT and it’s in. And if either the pale Festbier or the copper Märzen appears on a tap near you this fortnight, the app will show you where.
